en: Nāgānanda, Act One: The Benediction (Nāndī)

Resorting to the pretext of meditation, you contemplate some woman; yet, opening your eyes for a moment, though you are its protector, you do not save these people afflicted by the arrows of the God of Love.
You are a hypocrite in compassion; who else is more utterly merciless than you?
May the Victor, who was told by the daughters of Māra, "Be jealous! regarding his enlightenment, protect you.
Moreover—

by the heroic Māras, who have drawn their bows with desire and possess slain, clever, and leaping [powers], and by the divine host of women, whose eyes move with smiles, yawns, and the knitting of eyebrows;

May the Lord of Sages protect you— he who was seen by Vāsava, his body thrilled with wonder, as he meditated on the attainment of unshakable awakening, while the Siddhas bowed their heads in reverence.
Śrīharṣa is a skillful poet, this assembly is appreciative of merit, the life of the Bodhisattva is captivating to the world, and we are experts in drama;
when even each one of these factors individually is a ground for attaining the desired fruit, how much more so when they are all combined?
Through the accumulation of extraordinary fortune, this entire multitude of virtues has arisen.
O friend of the twice-born, your attendants, and your kin; O female swan at the lake of my abode, you of gentle character;
O noble one, a lotus to the moon of other men—first of all, you must do this.
In order to perform service for my parents, I shall abandon my inherited sovereignty and go to the forest this very day, just as Jīmūtavāhana did.
"I know it to be the seat of passion, yet I have no conviction that it will perish; who on earth does not know that it is averse to discerning what ought and ought not to be done?
Thus, even though this youth under the sway of the senses is so censurable, it may still lead to pleasure."
If my parents go [to heaven] in this very way through my devotion while I am serving them.

Does he shine before his father while standing on the ground as much as he does on a lion-throne? Is the pleasure he feels while massaging his father’s feet found in a royal assembly? Is the satisfaction he derives from consuming the three worlds equal to that which comes from eating what has been left over by his guru?
Indeed, ruling a kingdom is nothing but toil; is there any virtue whatsoever in that which has abandoned its heavy burdens? // Nā_1.7 //

The subjects have been established on the path of righteousness and settled in happiness; likewise, his kinsmen have been brought to a state of equality with himself, and protection has been ensured for the kingdom.
Furthermore, he has granted to the supplicant the wish-fulfilling tree itself, yielding fruits exceeding even their most cherished desires.
Tell me, what should be done after this, or whatever else resides in your mind?
The ocean was struck by its waves, causing the sandalwood trees to drip with resin as they were rubbed against the temples of the intoxicated world-elephants; its mountain caves resounded with cries,
and its pearl-beds were stained red by the lac-dye from the footprints of the Siddha women as they walked there.
This Malaya mountain is to be resorted to; it somehow makes my heart restless.
My right eye throbs; I have no desire for any fruit whatsoever.
Yet the word of the Sage cannot be false—what could this be?
For the sake of clothing, tree bark not too wide has been cut out of sheer compassion;
waterfalls provide clear, sky-like water for broken and worn-out water-pots;
and here and there, girdles made of muñja grass, snapped and cast aside, are seen by the young students.
And by the parrot, through constant listening, this verse of the Sāmans is being recited: // Nā_1.11 //
They seem to offer a sweet welcome with the humming of bees, and they perform a salutation with their heads bowed down by fruit;
scattering showers of flowers, they seem to be offering me the traditional water of respect.
How is it that even the trees have been taught the honoring of guests?

Manifesting a clear distinction between low and high pitches through their mastery of musical positions, they blend the sound of their strings with the resonance of the lute as if with the humming of bees;
meanwhile, these [elephants] have silenced the sound of chewing mouthfuls of grass held between their tusks.
With their limbs gracefully extended, the deer listen to the song with its clearly articulated and charming cadences.
O Gaurī, whose radiance is as white as the pollen of the filaments of a full-blown lotus! O Blessed One, may my heart's desire be fulfilled.
By your grace.
Here, by means of this tenfold *vyañjana-dhātu* (articulatory element) which has been acquired, this *laya* (tempo) is clearly manifested in three ways— fast, medium, and slow—
and the three *yatis* (caesuras), beginning with the "cow's tail" (*gopuccha*), are likewise accomplished in sequence.
Furthermore, the three methods of instrumental music, which follow the flood of reality, have been correctly demonstrated.
If she were a celestial nymph, the thousand eyes of Indra would have achieved their purpose;
if she were a serpent-maiden, the netherworld would be empty while her face remains here;
and if she were a Vidyadhari, our entire race would have triumphed over all other species.

If there were one born of a lineage of perfected beings (siddha) who were established as perfected beings throughout the three worlds, then [the existence of such a lineage] would be proven. // 1.16 //
O you with tremulous, long eyes;

O you with full, firm breasts shaken by your sighs; O you who cause such agitation—why does this slender body of yours, which has already attained the impurity of exhaustion through asceticism alone, now suffer further? Nāgārjuna 1.17.
This usnīṣa shines clearly upon his head; this ūrṇā between his eyebrows is radiant; his eye resembles a red lotus; his chest vies with that of Hari;
and since these two feet bear the marks of wheels, I believe he must be someone extraordinary.
He does not rest until he has attained the rank of a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas.

On one side is the word of my teacher, and on the other are the joys of seeing my beloved; weighed down by this conflict between going and not going, my heart still wavers even today. (Nāgānanda 1.19)
On one side is the word of my teacher, and on the other are the pleasures of beholding my beloved;
even now, my heart wavers, mounted upon the oscillation of going and coming.
By her, who is slow-moving due to the fullness of her hips,
my heart has been stepped upon even as she was walking elsewhere.
Carrying two temples white with the sandalwood paste rubbed off at that very moment from the heat,
his face being fanned by the breezes from his own flapping ears,
he now sprinkles the drops released from his trunk upon her heart, which has been especially moistened— [...by the tears of joy. (Verse 12)
The lord of elephants assumes a state that is as difficult to endure as a deep and lingering fever.
Thus ends the first act.
The second act begins:
You make even this [place] cool through contact with the sprouts of dense sandalwood creepers.
By your very sighs, you alone make the breeze through the *kadali* leaves warm. (Nāgānanda 2.1)
Because she turned back at the hermitage with the luster of her dark and white eyes— making the trees appear as if their branches were draped with shimmering black antelope skins—
I was struck by that very sight even in the presence of the sage.
O Puṣpeṣu, why are these arrows being discharged by you in vain? // Nā_2.2 //
Have nights not been spent, white with the moon; have blue lotuses not been smelled;
have the evening breezes, fragrant with blooming jasmine, not been endured;
or has the humming of bees in the lotus pond not been heard by me?
Why do you, without any pretense, address me as "unsteady" when I am in such distress?
How can I— who have not been withstood by a woman's heart, nor even by the flower-arrows cast by the Bodiless One—
be called "steadfast," when I speak of myself as such before you this very day?
This sandalwood bower, though its stones are set with moonstones, is not dear to me when deprived of her moon-like face,
just as the night’s sky is not dear when devoid of moonlight.
This is that very moonstone slab upon which, with her face pale and resting on her left sprout-like hand, she lets forth heavy sighs;
while I linger long, she makes her intention clear by the slight quivering of her eyebrows.
With my anger and mental agitation stilled, I beheld my beloved weeping.
By this rising moon of your face,
this surface of moonstone is as if being sprinkled with the water of your tears.
The mere outline of the beloved’s face— possessing the beauty of an unstained reflection and providing a festival for the eyes like the moon— brings joy even at its first sight.
This beloved is indeed present before me, established here by my own imagination;
if I were to look at her again and again and paint her, what wonder would there be in that? (Nāgārjuna 2.9)
For he is the ornament of the lineage of the Vidyādharas, wise, honored by the virtuous,
peerless in beauty, rich in prowess, learned, humble, and youthful;
and he who, striving for the welfare of sentient beings, would even abandon his own life out of compassion.
The thieves gave him their peerless sister; for me, there was both joy and sorrow. (Nāgārjuna 2.10)
"Truly, truly, O innocent one, such a rash act must not be done; remove this hand of yours, which resembles a sprout, from the creeper."
How can he who, I believe, is not even capable of plucking a flower, employ a noose for the purpose of hanging you? // Nā_2.11 //
How can this hand of yours, which has committed an offense by placing a noose upon my neck—a neck worthy of a garland of pearls—be released? How can it be set free?
In this Malaya mountain, bearing a luster like that of saffron powder due to the rain,
instantly surpassing the beauty of the twilight glow at the start of the day with its [red] hue,
and delightful with the sounds of the jingling anklets on the moving feet of women rising up—
The world of the Siddhas announces the time for bathing in the Rūdvāha river for your success.

I believe that the union of only certain fortunate individuals occurs when they have seen one another, possess similar forms, share mutual affection, and belong to the same family and age. (Nāgārjuna 2.14)
Thus ends the second act.
The third act:
He who constantly drinks wine and who brings about the pleasure of people...
The two great gods are indeed Balarāma and Kāmadeva. (Nāgārjuna 3.1)
In whose mouth the beloved placed a lotus-stalk as a toothpick, and in whose head wine was poured, and who always wore a crest-ornament upon his head. (Nāgānanda 3.2)
O Nomālikā, he who is so arrogant that he does not even know how to bow before Hari, Hara, and the Grandfather (Brahmā)—
that very Śekhara falls at your feet.
Upon being seen, she casts her gaze downward; when addressed, she offers no reply;
on the bed, she remains turned away; when embraced by force, she trembles;
and as her female companions depart from the dwelling, she strives only to go out after them.
"Today my newly-wedded beloved has become all the more a source of joy to me precisely because of her perversity."
O beloved, that I maintained silence in response to you while uttering the sound "huṃ," that this body of mine was scorched by the heat of forest fires as well as by the rays of the moon,
and that I spent so many days and nights with a deeply bowed mind in meditation— [all these were for your sake].
"This face which I now behold is the fruit of that asceticism of yours."
Is the weight of your breasts already enough to cause you fatigue, so why this other necklace at your waist?
Your pair of thighs is exhausted by the burden of your hips; why then this girdle? Your feet have no strength to carry even your thighs—whence these anklets?
You are already ravished by your own limbs; why do you wear ornaments that lead only to suffering?
The oozing sap of sandalwood trees cools the interior of the vine-arbors;
near the floors of the shower-houses, the peacock performs its dance to the sound of the waterfalls;
and water released from the machines rushes with speed through the trunks of the trees, filling their basins.
This flood of water, yellowish-brown with the pollen of flowers gathered effortlessly by its sudden onset, is not [the work of a god].
Moreover—
these grounds of the vine-arbors, made resonant by the beginning of songs,
possess the pollen of flowers that brings about a manifest contact with fine perfumes.
Drinking their fill of sweet nectar together with their companions, the bees seemed to be performing a drinking festival on all sides.
Their limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood paste, wearing garlands of *santānaka* flowers, and their pure white silken garments variegated by the intermingling radiance of ruby ornaments,
these [gods] drink honey-wine together with the Siddhas— the wine remaining after it has been tasted by their beloveds.
Gathering together in the shade of sandalwood trees, the Vidyādharas drink [the nectar].
This face of my beloved, having surpassed the moon with the luster of its cheeks,
now surely seeks to conquer the lotus, which is already overcome by the heat [of the sun].
This face of yours, with its playful eyebrows and coral-red sprout-like lips, is the Nandana garden; any other than this is merely a forest.
This blossoming of a smile is seen upon your sprout-like lower lip; but its fruit, O lovely-eyed one, is elsewhere—for me who gaze with my eyes. (Nāgārjuna 3.12)
O charming girl, this sacrifice bears a deep crimson luster brushed by the rays of the sun, its filaments made manifest by the spreading rays of her teeth.
Ah! This is the sacrifice! O innocent one!
It is true that your honey is equal to the lotus, O bee; however, while drinking from it, you do not appear to be so. // Nā_3.13 //
Without having slain that rival, how indeed shall I, shameless as I am, say to Jīmūtavāhana, "Your kingdom has been seized by the enemy"?
With their celestial chariots moving in every direction, traversing the entire path of the sky,
they create a darkening of the day like the monsoon season when the sun's rays are shrouded;
yet, having received your command here, they have now departed immediately, prepared for battle.
And may your own kingdom be accomplished, with its kings bowed down by the destruction of their arrogant enemies and their fear dispelled.

Know that even alone, with the mass of my sword-blade’s rays flashing like a mane as I have impetuously drawn it, I shall fall upon this wretched Matanga in battle like a lion upon a lordly elephant. (Nāgārjuna 3.16)

How could he who, out of compassion, would indeed give even his own body for the sake of another unasked, ever consent to the cruelty of killing living beings for the sake of a kingdom? (Nāgārjuna 3.17)

Having dispelled sleep from the lotuses by binding them with his seal (mudrā) and incessantly drawing [nectar] from the blossoming flowers, he who gladdens the entire universe with his own rays intent solely on fulfilling the hopes [of beings],
was seen even as he was setting by the Siddhas, whose mouths were made resonant with continuous hymns of praise.
Vivasvat alone is praiseworthy, for his exertion was solely for the sake of benefiting others.
Thus ends the third act.
The fourth act: Chamberlain—

Having established a fixed order for the women of the inner apartments and guarding against lapses at every step, I now, afflicted by old age, imitate the entire conduct of the king through the administration of punishment. (Nāgārjuna 4.1)
The bed is the grassy meadow, the seat a pure rock, the dwelling beneath the trees, the drink is cool water from mountain cascades, the food is edible roots, and the companions are the deer;
in this forest where every necessity is obtained without seeking, there is only this one drawback.
For those who seek what is difficult to attain, it is a waste to remain idle while their efforts for the sake of others' welfare are fruitless.

Just as this sound rises up loudly, piercing the path of hearing, so too does it resound through all the interior regions of mountain caves, intensified by the continuous and impetuous splashing of the lordly elephants plunging into the water.
For the most part, this tide approaches, white as countless swaying conch shells.
This shore of the ocean shines, suffused with the luster of gems, by its waters fragrant with camphor, cloves, and the ichor of elephants and sea-monsters.
Among his two thousand tongues, is there not even a single tongue by which he might say today,
"I have given my own self to the enemy of the earth for the sake of protecting a single snake"?
Thus, according to the arrangement established by the Lord of Serpents, those serpent-lords whom the King of Birds devours— whether they have gone,
are going, or will go in days to such increase— that these heaps of bones, white as the snowy mountains, belong to them.
For the sake of even this tiny body— a storehouse of all impurities, ungrateful, and perishable— fools commit sinful deeds.
When impermanence first embraces a newborn as its own,
just as a nurse does for a mother’s child, what room is there then for grief?
Who was the savior for you as you, bewildered and shedding a continuous stream of tears, uttered many lamentations, casting your piteous gaze in all directions while crying, "O my little son!";
yet you abandoned this infant resting in your mother's lap, consuming a lack of compassion?
I believe the heart of the lord of birds was not made of adamant, for it was shattered by the thunderbolt. 9.

Those holy ones have passed away—those who, being exceedingly compassionate, never made the prayers of supplicants fruitless; who, out of their embrace of mercy, did not count their own self-interest when it came to the welfare of others;
and whose minds were perpetually pained by the suffering of others.
O Mother, restrain the force of your tears now; before whom are you weeping?

If I do not rescue this man who is distressed, whose life-breath has reached his throat, and who has been abandoned by his own kinsmen, then what benefit is there for me in this body? (Nāgārjuna 4.11)
Beholding her, I think that out of affection for her son, even one with a heart of stone—even the enemy of serpents—would feel compassion. (Nāgārjuna 4.12)
Where is that Garuḍa, whose fierce beak was smeared with streaks of blood released from the splitting of the great serpent’s brain;
and where indeed is this virtuous one, whose form and appearance possess such a gentle nature? // Nā_4.13 //
"Mother, hand over this mark of execution to me; having covered it, I shall give my own body to the son of Vinatā so that your son's life may be preserved. (Nāgārjuna 4.14)
In former times, Viśvāmitra, like a dog-cooker, ate dog-flesh for whose sake Nādijaṅgha was slain by Gautama after having performed that service;
and for whose sake Tārkṣya, the son of Kaśyapa, eats serpents every day.
That virtuous person who, out of compassion, gives away his very life-breaths for the sake of others as if they were a blade of grass.
Beings like me, mere insignificant creatures, are born and die;
but whence is the birth of those like you, who have girded their loins for the sake of others?
She dies when you die; she lives while you live.
If you desire her to remain alive, protect yourself by means of my life-breaths.
In this place, where dense darkness is created by vultures whose greed increases as they seize morsels of flesh dropped from their flickering beaks while they flap their two wings,
rows of jackal tongues fall with a *chham* sound, tossed up from their mouths.
They resound within the putrid, thick-smelling fat that flows incessantly from the streams of flesh.
This cremation ground is as fierce as a body with a skull-bowl white as the moon, where the Vināyakas find delight through their daily consumption of the flesh of the unburied dead.
In whichever state of existence we may be born, O dear child, may you alone be our mother in each and every one of them. (Nāgārjuna 4.20)
This pair of red garments, obtained when Āla arrived, brings great joy to one who casts off the body for the sake of another. (Nāgārjuna 4.21)
Rows of wings, resembling the clouds that bring the end of an eon, cover the sky;

on the shore, a wind of great force hurls the water as if to churn the ocean of the earth. Instantly causing fear by evoking the suspicion of the world's destruction, it is gazed upon with terror by the lords of the elephants of the quarters.
The radiance of his body, possessing the brilliance of twelve suns, repeatedly reddens the ten directions.
I do not think that Malayavatī, moist with the juice of Malaya sandalwood,
brings such pleasure as this stone for execution does when embraced for the sake of accomplishing one's desired goal.
That confidence which was not obtained by me in childhood while sleeping trustingly on my mother’s lap—
that happiness has been found by me upon the lap of this stone of execution.
Having cast his reflection into the moon, that embodiment of Śeṣa, moving in a circle that caused fear,
was seen by his elder brother as the sun trembled from the terror of the chariot horses;
he appeared like one whose wings were outstretched by the masses of clouds clinging to the horizon.
In an instant, he reached the Malaya mountain, which was eager to swallow the great serpent.
By protecting this serpent today, whatever merit has been earned by me through the gift of my own body— by that,
in birth after birth, may my acquisition of a physical form always be for the sake of others alone.
Having now pierced this man fallen upon the execution stone with my beak— fiercer than a thunderbolt— to protect the remaining serpents,
I shall swiftly uproot this serpent, who is clothed in red garments, to devour him.
It was smeared as if with the blood trickling from his heart, which was being torn apart by the fear of me.

"Is this a rain of flowers falling from the sky, delighting the bees with its fragrance? Or is this the sound of celestial drums resonating in all directions, as if in heaven? Ah, I understand! I believe even that Pārijāta tree has been shaken by the wind of my speed."
All the clouds of universal destruction, fearing the onset of dissolution, have also roared.
Just as this teacher shines as the protector of the nāgas,
even so will he clearly dispel today the desire of the serpent-eater.
Thus ends the fourth act. The fifth act begins with the Chamberlain: Chamberlain:—
Even toward a loved one who has come to one's own home garden, evil is suspected out of affection;
how much more so toward one situated in the midst of a terrifying wilderness where many calamities have been witnessed?
Wearing a silken garment with wavy borders resembling foamy water,
and accompanied by his noble and highly meritorious queen of equal age,
this Jīmūtaketu possesses a splendor truly worthy of the ocean.
Near whom this Malayavatī shines like the shore.
The pleasures of youth have been enjoyed, fame has been spread abroad,
the kingdom has been maintained with a steady mind, and even austerity was practiced;
there is a praiseworthy son born of a worthy lineage, and this daughter-in-law is his peerless match.
O Māyā, death is indeed to be contemplated today by one who has achieved his purpose.
"Why do you throb again and again in my left eye, O right eye, indicating some misfortune for me?
Your throbbing has been rendered fruitless by my ruined sight; my son is safe. (Nāgārjuna 5.4)

Is this something falling suddenly from the sky before us—releasing rays of its own blood-red splendor that cause intense pain to the eyes of the onlookers, appearing like stars torn asunder by a cataclysmic wind? // Nā_5.5 //
As numerous serpents are being devoured by Tārkṣya,
their crest-jewels fall down in this manner, appearing like meteors.
Having quickly prostrated at Gokarṇa on the shore of the ocean, I indeed reached that place which is the ground where serpents cannot be slain;
seizing that Vidyādhara, whose body was covered with wounds from my claws and beak, Garuḍa soared into the sky.
I have gained neither fame through protection nor the praiseworthy fulfillment of my master’s command;
having given myself up, I am now being protected by another—alas, what a pity! Woe is me! How bitter it is!
I have been deceived, I have been deceived!

At first, it is a heavy downpour upon the earth; then, as it falls more sparsely, it becomes large drops; thereafter, falling upon stones, it shatters into thin, scattered droplets; then it scatters over the ground, crawling with insects;
on a wall of mineral ore, it is difficult to perceive; and on the peak of a mountain, it takes the form of a thick, dark blue mass.
O Tārkṣya, desiring to see Menā, I go following the stream of blood with great care.
"O son, tell me your own suffering, which is so difficult to bear; let it be transferred to me, so that it may become endurable for you. (Nāgārjuna 5.10)
"My life was preserved by a certain Vidyādhara whose mind was filled with compassion, who gave himself to Garuḍa. (Nāgānanda 5.11)
Even though you have departed for another world, you have not abandoned the path of propriety by casting your crest-jewel at my feet.

As I perpetually prostrate my two feet with devotion, bowing my supple head so very low, how is it that the crest-jewel—though softened by constant friction against them—is not merely harmless, but rather violently tears at my heart? How can this be?
Making the mountain slopes appear like valleys with the scratches of his beak wet with blood,
his inner space scorched by the rows of flame-like rays from his own eyes,
and the earth deeply penetrated by the tips of his claws as terrible as a thunderbolt ready to strike— Please perform the translation.
This enemy of the serpents is seen from afar upon the very peak of Mount Malaya.
There is no exhaustion even for this ocean of fortitude, though he drinks excessive blood;
his face remains serene despite enduring the pains born of having his flesh cut away.
That his body has not withered is clearly evident by the visible horripilation upon it.
His gaze falls even upon his benefactor as if it were his wrongdoer.
Blood still flows from the openings of my veins, and the mass of flesh remains within my body;
yet I see no sign of your satisfaction. O Garuḍa, why have you ceased eating? // Nā_5.16 //
"By this fortitude, you have again won over our very hearts, even as I drew blood from your heart with my beak. (Nāgārjuna 5.17)
Let alone the svastika mark upon your chest; no bodice is seen upon your body.
Even as I speak, you have not counted even these two tongues of mine;
for there are three [fires], the luster of whose jewels emerges under the guise of dense clouds of smoke from the fire of fierce poison.
Do you not see these hoods, swollen by the winds of your unbearable, hissing sighs of grief? // Nā_5.18 //
In the caves of Mount Meru, on the slopes of the Himavat, on Mount Mahendra,
upon the rocky surfaces of Kailāsa, and even in the regions of the Malaya ridges—
in all those various places, I have heard it many times.
His fame was being sung aloud by hosts of those investigating the worlds and the non-worlds.
"Is it right for you to take me from the depths of Pātāla to this world, while you yourself have protected your own body from Tārkṣya by means of my body? (Nā_5.20)
How indeed could this distinction between "one's own" and "another" be true for one whose very nature is compassion?
Why did such a thought not arise in you: "Which shall I protect—the many, or the one?"—when you sacrificed your own life to save a snake from Tārkṣya?
By him, this entire family—himself, his parents, and his wife—has been utterly destroyed.
With his flickering tongues of flame, resembling the tips of the tongue of Time as it moves in the act of devouring the three worlds,

he is capable of swallowing the seven oceans like mouthfuls of clarified butter; and when the oceans are milked by the very winds of his own wings, which are more powerful than the onset of cataclysmic tempests—
I fall into the submarine fire at the end of the eon, which causes terror with its blazing flames.

Seeing my son, his remaining limbs mangled, as if departing for the region of the throat due to having no refuge, and now relinquishing his life-breaths— how is it that I, a sinner, do not shatter into a hundred pieces?
In this thing called a "body," which is a mass of fat, bone, flesh, marrow, and blood, covered by skin and always loathsome to behold—what beauty can there be? (Nāgārjuna 5.24)
Constantly refrain from harming living beings; feel remorse for what you have done in the past;

and with effort, accumulate a stream of merit by granting fearlessness to all sentient beings, so that the sin arising from the injury of living creatures, once it has ripened, may not bear fruit here.
Like a *pala* of salt cast into the unfathomable flood of water within a deep lake.
Slumbering in the sleep of ignorance, I have been awakened by you;
from this day forward, I shall desist from the slaughter of all living beings.
In some places he has the form of a continent with vast masses of coils like sandbanks; in other places, his body is encircled by the illusion of whirlpools;
and in some places, moving from bank to bank, he is like a bridge.
May the assembly of nāgas dwell happily in the great ocean.

Carrying masses of hair resembling thick darkness, with locks drooping and hanging down to their feet, and with cheeks reddened by the first touch of the sun’s rays as if smeared with vermilion, they—
though their limbs were languid from exertion— disregarded their pain while in the sandalwood forest.
In this [lake], let the young female nāgas sing with passion this very fame of yours.
Surely your mother, pained by the sorrow of your suffering, remains there imagining you torn apart by the tip of Tārkṣya’s beak. (Nāgārjuna 5.29)
These limbs no longer possess consciousness; my ear does not hear for long the words of distinct syllables.
Alas! This eye has suddenly closed;
O Father, these breaths of mine depart while I am helpless.
Without its support, where shall fortitude go for refuge? Who here is capable of bearing patience? Whose devotion to generosity has ceased?
Truth is slain; where shall poor truthfulness go now? And where is compassion today?
The world that has come into being is empty now that you, O son, have passed away to another world.

The Lord of Waters, whose wings were raised aloft by winds impelled with exceeding speed, caused the twelve suns along with their fires to fall down, distressed by fainting from the scorching of his eye-fire;
meanwhile, he pulverized with his beak the thunderbolt of Indra, the mace of Kubera, and the staff of Yama, the Lord of the World of the Dead.
Having utterly defeated the gods in battle, I shall for a moment pour forth a rain consisting of nectar.
This crown-protrusion shines clearly upon your head; this ūrṇā-hair between the eyebrows is radiant;
your eyes resemble the lotus; your chest vies with the moon;
and your feet are marked with the wheel-sign—nevertheless, alas, my child, how is it that through my own misdeeds...?
You shall not rest until you have attained the rank of a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas.
"O child Jīmūtavāhana, I am well-pleased with you, who have benefited the worlds even at the cost of your own life; live on! Nāgānanda 5.34.
O you who grant boons exceeding what is desired, O remover of the suffering of those who prostrate before you, O refuge, O you honored by the supreme vidyās, I bow to your feet.
Gaurī. // Nā_5.35 //
Having attained their full bodies, with limbs raised high and radiant with the jewels on their expanded hoods,
licking the earth with the tips of their two tongues out of greed for the taste of nectar— these serpents now possess a gathered momentum like the surging floods of the river from Mount Malaya.
By crooked paths of departure, the lords of venomous serpents enter the mass of water.
Having personally consecrated herself with these most purifying waters— frequenting swans, free from the stain of contact with lotus pollen, arisen from my own mind,
and brought forth at will— poured from jeweled jars fashioned by her own desire;
I shall, out of affection, instantly make you the universal monarch of the Vidyādharas.
"O Cakravartin, let this golden-footed elephant advance, and this white elephant with four tusks; and Śyāma, Hari, and Malayavatī as well—having beheld these jewels of yours. (Nāgārjuna 5.38)
This Śaṅkhacūḍa has been saved from the face of the Lord of Birds; Vainateya has been subdued by him, and all those lords of serpents who were previously devoured have also been restored to life.
By the recovery of my life, his vital breaths were not lost to his elders, and he has attained the status of a universal monarch.
O Goddess, you have been seen in person; what further beloved thing could possibly be requested beyond this? (Nāgārjuna 5.39)
May the clouds, bearing the dance of joyful peacocks, release rain in due season;
may they clothe the earth in the upper garment of lush, continuous greenery.
May those free from calamity, gathering their merits with hearts devoid of malice, [attain their goal].
And may the subjects always find delight in the company of kinsmen and friends.
May there be auspiciousness for all the world; may the hosts of beings be devoted to the welfare of others;
may faults go to their destruction; and may the world be happy everywhere.
Thus ends the fifth act.
